summary:
Distrito Federal stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition, while calling on those without such procedures to adopt them and warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Lethal violence against trans people in the capital is recorded at a level that leads the country. An annual report by a Mexican LGBT+ news collective, published in May 2025, recorded 115 violent incidents against LGBT+ people across Mexico in 2024, of which 59 were killings; for the first time Mexico City returned the highest state count, with 17 homicides, 11 of them trans women. In January 2024 the activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca was shot dead in Mexico City, one of at least three transgender people killed in the opening weeks of that year, and the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

The local legislature has criminalised the killing of trans people as a distinct offence. On 18 July 2024 Mexico City's congress approved transfeminicidio in the local penal code, making the capital the second state in the country to typify the offence; the reform is known as the 'Paola Buenrostro law' after a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe such legislation as critical to their sense of safety. Article 148-Ter was added to the local code on 23 August 2024, defining transfeminicidio as the killing of a trans woman or feminine-spectrum person by reason of gender identity or expression, and the accompanying instrument FGJCDMX/04/2025 sets initial-response protocol rules for such cases alongside feminicide investigations.

Investigation practice has been reformed alongside the statute. In December 2024 Mexico City created a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit, whose investigators may no longer demand a legal name or gender change, or medical documentation, from trans people when handling cases.

Policing and protection machinery in the capital continues to expand. On 25 August 2025 the mayor of Mexico City launched the new Gender Police, with 30 patrol units to handle cases of violence against women and girls in the capital.

Partnership recognition is settled: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. The gap between statute and practice remains the standing caution for visitors. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.
tangentialFactors:
The capital's position sits within a national pattern of uneven provision rather than standing apart from it. Human Rights Watch reported in March 2025 that administrative gender recognition procedures differ sharply between Mexican states, and the May 2025 collective report shows the same unevenness in lethal violence: Mexico City's 17 LGBT+ homicides in 2024 were followed by Nuevo León with 5.

Mexico City's transfeminicidio statute is the second of its kind nationally, so at least one other state had already typified the offence before July 2024; the sources in this inventory do not name that state.

Document barriers elsewhere in Mexico illustrate what obstructed recognition costs. Human Rights Watch reported on 6 March 2024 that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, and set those barriers against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

National monitoring gives scale to the risk. Transgender Europe's records count 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100; Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.
localsOnly:
The Mexico City prison system has permitted same-sex conjugal visits since July 2007, a change introduced through the efforts of the National Human Rights Commission (CDHDF) under a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation. The visiting partner was not required to be married to the inmate, and the change applied to all prisons in Mexico City.

The dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit established in December 2024 constrains how prosecutors treat trans complainants and witnesses: investigators may no longer require proof of a legal name or gender change, or medical documentation, in the course of a case.

The transfeminicidio provision and its response protocol operate through local instruments of the Mexico City attorney general's office, so their procedural requirements bind local investigators rather than authorities in other states.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses how trans prisoners are housed in Mexico City: whether placement follows birth sex or stated identity, whether special units or segregation are used, and how the 2007 conjugal-visit policy interacts with trans inmates' housing classification remains unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory does not name the state that typified transfeminicidio before Mexico City in July 2024, so the identification of the first such jurisdiction is unresolved.

The prison conjugal-visit claim rests on a Wikipedia article accessed on 4 October 2026 rather than on the underlying 2003 statute or a prison authority record; the article itself gives no data on trans-prisoner practice.

Whether the Gender Police launched on 25 August 2025 receives trans-specific training, or how it handles cases involving trans victims, is not sourced in this inventory.

Enforcement data for the transfeminicidio provision after article 148-Ter took effect, including case numbers and outcomes, is not available in the sources provided.
